course.title: Probability and Statistics
course.description: Count what can happen. Change a condition, move an outlier, and test what a sample can tell you.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with arithmetic, fractions and the first Maths Foundations lessons.

paragraphs: Probability and statistics are two ways of dealing with uncertainty. Probability starts from a known setup, such as a fair die, and says how often each result should turn up. Statistics starts from the results, such as a list of bus delays or a survey of shoppers, and asks what they tell you. People study both because most decisions, from which bus to catch to whether a new medicine works, rest on numbers that vary.

The course has six lessons in two parts. The first part, Reasoning about chance, counts what can happen with coins and dice, shows how a clue changes the count, and finds the chance of several separate events happening together. The second part, Reading data, describes a list of numbers by its centre and its spread, and ends with what a sample of people or things can and cannot tell you about the whole group.
Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards, so a question only comes once you have been shown what it needs.
outcomes: You'll be able to find the probability of an event by counting equally likely outcomes.
You'll be able to say how a clue changes a probability, and work out the new value.
You'll be able to multiply the chances of independent events and tell them apart from events that cannot both happen.
You'll be able to find the mean and median of a list and say which one an extreme value moves.
You'll be able to measure how spread out a list is with the range and the standard deviation.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with fractions and decimals, and with the first lessons of Maths Foundations.

lessons.title: Count what can happen

lead.text: Start with the smallest case. Flip a coin twice and write down what you see, using H for heads and T for tails. The first flip can be H or T, and whichever it is, the second flip can be H or T as well. Written in order, the possible results are HH, HT, TH and TT. HT means heads on the first flip and tails on the second, so it is a different result from TH.

Each of those four results is an outcome: one complete way for the flips to turn out. A group of outcomes you care about is an event. “At least one head” is an event, and it holds three outcomes, HH, HT and TH.

Suppose the coin is fair, so that no outcome is favoured over another. The outcomes are then equally likely, and the chance of an event is its share of the list. Three of the four outcomes are in our event, so the probability of at least one head is 3 out of 4. Whenever every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes in it divided by the number of outcomes altogether.
That sentence is the method for the whole lesson. The only hard part is the counting, and the rest of the lesson is about counting when the list is too long to write out.
Try the same method on a different event with the same two coins. List the outcomes first, then count the ones that match.

Coins give a list short enough to write on one line. Dice do not. Roll one die and then another, and the first can show any of six numbers, with the second free to show any of six after it. Writing every pair out would be slow, so we draw a grid: the first roll runs down the side and the second runs along the top, so each cell holds one pair.

Order matters. A 1 on the first die and a 6 on the second is the cell (1,6). A 6 first and a 1 second is the cell (6,1), which sits somewhere else in the grid. Both are outcomes, and every cell is as likely as any other, because each die is fair.

afterFigure.text: The shaded cells in the picture are the pairs that add up to 7. We come back to them shortly. For now the useful fact is the shape of the grid. It always has one row for each face of the first die and one column for each face of the second, so dice with a different number of faces make a grid of a different size. Count along a row and down a column, and you know how many outcomes there are.

lead.text: Each cell of the grid is one ordered outcome. Look at how the grid is built before you answer.

reveal.text: Six rows of six cells. (1,6) and (6,1) sit in different cells, so both are counted.

lead.text: Now we can use the grid. The shaded cells are the pairs that add up to 7, running along the diagonal from (1,6) to (6,1). There are six of them, and every cell is equally likely. The chance of a total of 7 is the shaded share of the grid: 6 out of 36, which simplifies to 1 in 6.

Compare a total of 2. Only one pair makes it, the double (1,1), so its share is 1 out of 36. The list of possible totals runs neatly from 2 to 12, and it is tempting to think each total is as likely as the next. They are not. A total gets its chance from the number of cells that lead to it, and the totals in the middle have the most cells.

afterFigure.text: Move the total on the picture and watch the shaded cells grow towards 7 and shrink again after it. That pattern is why 7 is the favourite in every dice game.

lead.text: Compare the corner of the grid, where both dice show 1, with the shaded diagonal.

steps.headline: Find the probability that two dice total 8.

workedSteps.text: Go along the first rolls and find the partner each one needs. A first roll of 2 needs a 6, and a first roll of 3 needs a 5.
Count all the pairs that make 8.
Divide by all 36 pairs.

lead.text: So far an event has been a single total. An event can also gather several totals. “A total of at least 11” means 11 or 12, and every pair that reaches either of them belongs to the event.

The counting goes the same way as before: add up the cells for each total in the event. A total of 11 has two cells, (5,6) and (6,5), and a total of 12 has one, (6,6). Together that is 3 cells, so the probability is 3 out of 36, which is 1 in 12.

afterFigure.text: The bottom of the fraction stays the whole grid, whatever the event is. Each cell has one total, so no cell can be counted twice. Move the total on the picture to see how the event grows as the limit comes down.

lead.text: An event can hold several totals. Count the cells for every total in it, then divide by the cells in the whole grid.

Every cell in the grid is either inside an event or outside it. Take “a total of at least 11” again. Its 3 cells are inside, and the other 33 cells are outside. The two groups share no cell, and together they fill the grid.

That gives a shortcut. The probability of the cells outside an event is 33 out of 36, and it equals 1 minus the probability of the event, because 1 stands for the whole grid. What an event leaves out is called its complement. When an event is large, counting its complement is often quicker than counting the event itself.
The question below asks about a total under 10, which is the complement of a total of at least 10. Questions that say “not” are often complements too.
Every pair either makes at least 10 or does not. No pair is in both groups, and together the two groups fill the grid.

reveal.text: You did not recount the grid. The cells outside the event are its complement, and the two probabilities add to 1.

blocks.text: Pick up almost any board game and you will find two dice in the box. You shake them and let go, and everyone leans in to see the total. After a few games you start to notice something. A 7 turns up all the time, and a 2 hardly ever does. Players who have never studied chance plan around that, and they are right to.

The feeling can be made exact. A fair die has no memory and no favourites, so what two dice do on any throw is a matter of counting. If you can list everything the dice might show, you can say how often each total will come up, and you can say it before the dice leave your hand.
This lesson does the listing. It begins with two coins, because a list of four things is easy to hold in your head. Then it moves to two dice, where the list grows into a grid of pairs.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the chance of a dice total by counting, and see why 7 turns up more often than 2.

recap.keyIdea: When outcomes are equally likely, a probability is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the number of all outcomes.

blocks.text: You began with two coins and four outcomes, then built a grid for two dice. Six of its cells make a total of 7 and only one makes a 2, which is why 7 comes up so often. You counted 6 cells for at least 10 and found the other 30 by taking the complement.

recap.nextHook: That grid assumes you know nothing about the throw. When a friend glimpses one die and tells you something about it, part of the grid is no longer possible. The next lesson starts from there.

lessons.title: When the condition changes

lead.text: Take the two coin flips from the last lesson. Before anything is known there are four equally likely outcomes. Now a friend peeks and tells you that at least one coin landed heads. That is a clue, and it changes what could have happened. TT has no heads in it, so it cannot be what happened. We cross it off.

Three outcomes survive: HH, HT and TH. They were equally likely before the clue. Crossing one off gives the others no advantage, so they stay equally likely. One of the three is two heads, which makes the chance of two heads 1 out of 3. Before the clue it was 1 out of 4.

A chance worked out inside the shorter list is called a conditional probability. Questions about one often use the word “given”: the chance of two heads, given at least one head. The clue sets the bottom of the fraction, and the outcomes you want are counted inside the shorter list.
A friend rolls a die out of your sight. She tells you only that the result is even. Cross off the results that the clue rules out.

The same thing happens on the grid of two dice. Suppose the clue is that the first die showed 1 or 2. Every pair whose first die is larger has been ruled out. The grid is built with the first roll down the side, so a clue about the first die removes whole rows.

afterFigure.text: The faded rows in the picture are the ones the clue has ruled out. Only the bright rows are still in play, and from now on everything is counted inside them. Those cells are the new list of possible outcomes, in the same way that HH, HT and TH were the new list for the coins.

lead.text: The first die is known to be 1 or 2. Count what is left in the grid.

reveal.text: Two rows of six cells remain. The clue changed the number of possible outcomes from 36 to the count you found.

lead.text: With the clue in place, 12 pairs can still have happened. Suppose we want the chance that the second die shows at most 4, given that the first showed 1 or 2. Look only at the surviving rows. Each row has four cells with a second roll of 1, 2, 3 or 4, so the two rows hold 8 matching pairs. The probability is 8 out of 12, which is 2/3.
The bottom of the fraction is 12, not 36. The 24 pairs in the crossed-off rows cannot have happened, so they have no place in the count.

afterFigure.text: A clue can keep other rows. “The first die is at least 5” keeps the bottom two rows and rules out the other four. The method is the same whichever rows survive: shrink the grid to the rows that fit the clue, count the pairs in them, then count the ones you want.

steps.headline: Given a first roll of at most 2, find the probability of a second roll of at most 3.

workedSteps.text: Two rows survive, so 12 pairs are possible.
Count the pairs in those rows with a second roll of at most 3.
Divide by the 12 possible pairs.

lead.text: The clue and the question do not have to concern the same die. Keep the clue that the first die showed 1 or 2, and ask instead about the total. Suppose we want the chance of a total of at least 8.

In the first row, even a 6 on the second die only makes 7, so no pair there reaches 8. In the second row only (2,6) does. That is 1 pair out of the 12 that remain, which is 1/12. A small first die makes a high total hard to reach, and the number agrees.

afterFigure.text: The clue decides where to count. The event decides what to count there. Change either one and the answer changes, even though the grid underneath is the same.

lead.text: Now ask about a total of at least 7. Look only inside the rows the clue leaves, and divide by their pairs.
Suppose your friend gets a better look and says the first die was exactly 1. That is a tighter clue. Only the top row of the grid survives, so six pairs remain, one for each value of the second die.

afterFigure.text: In that row, the chance of a second roll of at most 3 is 3 out of 6, which is 1/2. A tighter clue leaves a shorter list, and each remaining pair carries more weight. All you need to ask is which second rolls fit the question.

lead.text: A tighter clue leaves less. The first die is known to be 1, so one row survives. Restrict first, then count the event inside it.

blocks.text: A friend rolls two dice under a cup and keeps the cup down. You are asked to bet on whether the total is 7 or more. With nothing to go on, the grid of pairs from the last lesson gives you the answer. Then she lifts the cup for a moment and you catch sight of the first die. It was small, a 1 or a 2, but you could not tell which.
That glimpse should change your bet. A small first die makes a high total harder to reach, though it is hard to say by how much without working it out.

A clue like that adds nothing to the grid. It takes things away. Some pairs can no longer have happened, and the chances have to be worked out among the pairs that remain. This lesson shows how, first with two coins and then with the dice under the cup.

intro.promise: By the end you'll cross out the outcomes a clue rules out, and find a chance among the ones that remain.

recap.keyIdea: A clue shrinks the list of possible outcomes. A conditional probability counts the favourable outcomes inside the shorter list and divides by its size.

blocks.text: You cut 36 pairs down to 12 once you knew the first die was at most 2. Inside those rows, 6 pairs have a second roll of at most 3. Only 3 reach a total of at least 7. A tighter clue, a first roll of exactly 1, left a single row.

recap.nextHook: In every case so far a clue changed the chances. Sometimes a clue about one thing tells you nothing about another, as with a coin and a die. The next lesson starts there.

lessons.title: Independent repetitions

lead.text: Flip a coin, roll a die, and write down the pair, such as heads and 3. Heads can come with any of the six die numbers, and so can tails, so the pairs form a grid again, with the two coin results on one side and the six die numbers on the other.

The coin has no effect on the die. If a friend tells you the coin landed heads, the die is just as likely to show a 3 as it was before. Events like that are independent: learning that one has happened leaves the chance of the other unchanged.

That is different from the last lesson. There, hearing about the first die changed the chances for the total, because the total depends on both dice. Here the coin and the die share nothing, and that makes their chances easy to combine.
Think of the grid that a coin and a die make together. Each coin result can go with every die result.

Take heads and a 3. Every pair in the grid is equally likely, so the chance of this one is 1 out of 12. The same number comes from the separate chances. Heads has chance 1/2 and a 3 has chance 1/6, and 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.

A picture in words shows why. Half of all the coin results are heads, and of those, one sixth have a 3 on the die. A sixth of a half is a twelfth. For independent events, the chance that both happen is the product of their separate chances.

afterFigure.text: Two dice tell the same story. The square marks the pairs where both dice show 4 or less. Each die alone passes with 4 values out of 6, which is 2/3. The square is 4 cells by 4, which is 16 of the 36 cells and a probability of 16/36 = 4/9. Multiplying 2/3 × 2/3 gives 4/9 as well, so the product agrees with the count.

lead.text: The same picture works with a different cut-off. Both dice must show 3 or less, so the pairs form a smaller square.

reveal.text: The square is 3 cells by 3, so 9 of 36. Each die passes with chance 1/2, and 1/2 × 1/2 agrees with your count.

steps.headline: Find the probability that both dice show at most 2.

workedSteps.text: One die: find the chance of at most 2.
The dice are independent, so multiply the two chances.

lead.text: The rule has no limit. To find the chance that several independent events all happen, multiply the chance of each. Four coin flips that all land heads have chance 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/16. Each extra flip multiplies by another 1/2, so the chance halves every time.
The rule also does not care what kind of events they are. A coin and a die follow it, and so do two dice. Find the chance of each event by itself, then multiply.
The one thing to check first is that the events really are independent. Two rolls of a die are, because a die has no memory. A coin that has just landed heads is no more likely to land tails next.
Different kinds of event follow the same rule. Find each chance on its own, then combine them.

Independent events should not be confused with events that cannot both happen. Roll one die. “It shows a 1” and “it shows a 2” cannot both happen, because one roll gives one number. Events like that are mutually exclusive. They are not independent, because if you learn the die showed a 1 you know it did not show a 2, and the chance of the second falls to nothing. Independent events leave each other's chances alone, whereas exclusive events rule each other out.

Independence also gives a way to count “at least one”. Suppose you want the chance that at least one of two dice is above 4. Listing those pairs is awkward, but the event is everything except “both dice are 4 or less”. That second event has chance 4/9, found on the grid earlier, so the first has chance 1 − 4/9 = 5/9.
Back to two dice. “At least one is above 3” is easy to count the other way round, as everything except “both at most 3”.

reveal.text: You did not list the pairs. You took the complement of the both-low event, which independence let you find.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish independent events from mutually exclusive events, and calculate a joint probability.
lessons.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: Some board games start a turn with two things at once: toss a coin and roll a die, and you may move only if the coin shows heads and the die shows a six. The coin lands on the table. The die rolls somewhere else. Neither knows what the other did.

That is a different situation from the cup in the last lesson. A glimpse of one die changed the chances for the total, but nothing about the coin tells you anything about the die. When two things are separate like that, their chances are easy to combine, and the same rule works for batteries failing, machines breaking and shots going in.

This lesson finds the rule and checks it on a grid, so you can see why it works. It then looks at pairs of events that cannot happen together, which are easy to confuse with events that simply do not affect each other.

intro.promise: By the end you'll multiply the chances of separate events, and tell them apart from events that cannot both happen.

recap.keyIdea: When events are independent, the chance that both happen is the product of their chances. Events that cannot happen together are not independent.

blocks.text: You found that both dice at most 3 has chance 9/36, the same as 1/2 × 1/2. Then you used the rule on a coin and a die, and took the complement to find the chance that at least one of two dice is above 3.

recap.nextHook: So far chance has been about what might happen. The next lesson turns to numbers that have already happened, and asks which single number best describes a whole list of them.

lessons.title: Centre and outliers

lead.text: Back to the five friends and their receipts. To give one number for what each person spent, we need a value that stands in for the whole list. A number like that is a measure of the list's centre, and there is more than one way to find it.

The first way is to settle up fairly. Put all the money into one pot and share it back out, so that everyone ends with the same amount. Suppose three of the friends spent £3, £5 and £10. The pot holds £18, and shared three ways it comes to £6 each. That share is the mean: add up all the values, then divide by how many there are.

The mean uses every value in the list, so each one pulls on it. The £10 drags the mean up to £6, even though two of the three friends spent less. In everyday speech this is the average, though there are other kinds of average, which is why statisticians use the more exact name.
Use the sharing idea from the last screen on five friends instead of three.
The mean needs every number in the list. A second centre uses only their order. Put the values in order, smallest first. The one in the middle is the median.

Take the list 7, 2, 9, 4 and 5. In order it reads 2, 4, 5, 7, 9. There are five values, so the middle is the third one, with two values below it and two above. The median is 5. The order matters: the middle of the list as written is a 9, which is not the middle in size.

This makes the median a different kind of centre. It cares about where a value sits in the order and ignores how far the values lie from each other. Later in the lesson we will see what that does when one value is far from the rest.
Put these values in size order first, then pick out the middle one.

With five values there is one in the middle. With four there is not. Two values sit in the middle, with one value on each side of the pair. The median then falls halfway between them, so we take their average: add the pair and halve the total.

Take 3, 9, 5 and 7. In order they read 3, 5, 7, 9. The middle pair is 5 and 7. They add to 12, and half of 12 is 6. The median is 6. It is not one of the values in the list, which is fine, because it only has to sit between them.

afterFigure.text: The same two moves work for any list. Sort it, find the middle position, and if there are two middle values, average them.

workedSteps.text: Sort the values.
Four values have two in the middle: the second and third. Add them.
Halve that total to average the pair.

lead.text: Now for the question this lesson has been heading towards. Take the list 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Its mean is 3 and its median is 3. Let the last value grow while the others stay put. Use the slider under the picture to drag it upwards and watch the two centres.

afterFigure.text: Drag the 5 up to 50. The total grows by 45, so the mean grows by 9, from 3 to 12, which is higher than every other value in the list. The median is still the third value in order, and the third value has not moved, so it stays at 3.
A value that sits far from the rest of the list is an outlier. The mean follows an outlier because it uses every value. The median barely notices one, because it only looks at the order.

lead.text: The list is 2, 4, 4, 5 and 25, and the 25 is an outlier. Put the values in order and find the middle.

Which centre should you quote? It depends on what the number is for. If you want to share a total out evenly, the mean is the right one, because the total is what matters and every value should count.

If you want the typical value and the list has an outlier, the median usually describes it better. Take the yearly pay in a small firm, in thousands of pounds: 20, 22, 25, 26 and 107. The mean is 40, which is more than four of the five people earn, because one high salary drags it up. The median is 25, which is close to what most of them earn.
When a mean and a median are far apart, it is a sign that something in the list is pulling at one of them.
An estate agent wants the typical price from five recent sales, and one of them was a mansion. Choose the centre that the mansion cannot skew.

reveal.text: The median stays with the ordinary houses. The mean would have been dragged upwards by the mansion.
